headline: Democrats sweep the US midterms, rattling Wall Street and reshaping global politics — while the ASX had a strong day and Pilbara Minerals surged 8.9% on rising lithium prices.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara had its best session in a while, jumping 8.9% today. The catalyst appears to be a surge in lithium prices — US lithium giant Albemarle reported a 58% rise in energy storage sales on higher lithium prices, lifting sentiment across the whole sector. The long-term story here remains beaten-up but alive — the question is whether this is the start of a real recovery or just a bounce.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft dropped 2.7% in last night's session, its worst performer in the portfolio for the day. Two things hit it: a Business Insider report (backed by satellite imagery) suggesting Microsoft's $5 billion AI data centre spending is running behind schedule, and broader market selling after the Democrats' midterm win rattled tech investors uncertain about the new policy direction. The long-term AI growth story is intact — one rough night doesn't change that.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG had a solid session today, up 1.8%, riding the ASX 200's strong 2.6% gain. As a broadly diversified fund, it moves with the overall market and today's ASX rally lifted it nicely.

movers.name: DHHF (BetaShares Diversified All Growth ETF)
movers.note: DHHF climbed 1.6% today in line with the broader ASX rally. No specific news — this one just tracks the market, and the market was up solidly today.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS rose 1.6% on the ASX today, though this partly reflects the lag from US markets — VTS tracks the US total market, and reports suggest the US total market ETF (VTI equivalent) got a lift from initial post-midterm optimism before the NASDAQ sold off hard. Tonight's US session will be more telling.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI edged up 1.5% today. AI stocks generally got a mixed reception following the Democrats' midterm win — some traders sold on uncertainty about AI regulation policy, while others bought the dip. The ETF held up okay despite the broader tech wobble.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google slipped 1.7% last night. Bloomberg ran a notable piece arguing that Google's own AI products (like AI Overviews in Search) risk cannibalising its core ad revenue — essentially, the more people use AI answers, the less they click ads. That's a real long-term question, though the business remains enormously profitable.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE was the quiet achiever today, nudging up 0.5%. Emerging markets are watching the US midterm result carefully — a Democrat-controlled Congress is generally seen as more stable on trade policy, which is a mild positive for emerging market economies.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two edged up 1.2% last night, bucking the broader tech sell-off. GTA 6 news kept the stock in positive territory — the CEO publicly defended the game's delay, saying they didn't want a Cyberpunk 2077 situation (a game that launched broken and had to be recalled). Patient investors seem to be buying the story.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX surges 8.9% — is lithium finally turning?
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals had a massive day, up nearly 9% on the back of Albemarle (the world's biggest lithium producer) reporting a 58% jump in energy storage sales on higher lithium prices. You're still down 58% on this position overall, so this is early days. For a long-term holder, the thesis is starting to show signs of life — but it's not time to call a full recovery yet. Hold and watch closely this week.

watch_today.title: MSFT drops 2.7% last night — data centre concerns and midterm jitters
watch_today.detail: Microsoft had a rough night. Business Insider reported (with satellite images) that its $5 billion AI data centre build-out is behind schedule, and broader tech selling after the Democrats' midterm win added to the pressure. You're still up 22% overall on this position. Nothing has broken in the long-term story — Microsoft remains the AI infrastructure leader. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: GOOG down 1.7% — but the real question is its AI cannibalisation risk
watch_today.detail: Bloomberg published a thoughtful piece last night arguing that Google's own AI search features could eat into its ad revenue over time — if users get answers from AI instead of clicking links, Google makes less money. This is a genuine long-term risk worth watching, not just noise. You're down 8% overall on this position. Hold for now — the business is still a cash machine — but keep an eye on how Google addresses this in coming quarters.

watch_today.title: US midterms: Democrats win big — what it means for your US holdings tonight
watch_today.detail: The Democrats swept the midterms, taking control of Congress. Markets initially rallied but then sold off hard — the NASDAQ fell 4.1% and the S&P 500 dropped 2.6% last night. Your US-exposed holdings (MSFT, GOOG, TTWO, VTS.AX) will face some headwinds. The midterm result puts a lame-duck Trump in a weakened position, which creates policy uncertainty. Watch how US markets open tonight (from ~11:30pm AEST) for direction.

watch_today.title: RBA hikes rates again — big banks pass it on
watch_today.detail: The RBA has lifted the cash rate again and Australia's big banks have already passed the full increase on to mortgage holders. The RBA's deputy governor has conceded the central bank is 'losing Australians' trust' to manage inflation — a rare admission. For your portfolio, higher rates are a mild headwind for growth stocks and ETFs, but as a long-term holder, stay the course.

watch_today.title: Oil spikes to $90 — Middle East conflict escalates
watch_today.detail: Crude oil jumped 2.4% to $90.21/barrel last night as a third tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz amid the ongoing Iran conflict. The Strait of Hormuz is where about 20% of the world's oil passes through — any disruption there sends prices up fast. Higher oil prices feed into inflation, which complicates the RBA's rate decisions. Something to keep an eye on.

world.summary: The US midterm elections dominated global news overnight, with Democrats delivering a sweeping victory that sent shockwaves through markets, reshaped Middle East policy expectations, and left the Trump administration in a significantly weakened position. Meanwhile, Iran's war in the Strait of Hormuz is pushing oil to $90 a barrel.

stories.title: Democrats sweep US midterms in historic result
stories.why_it_matters: The Democrats pulled off what analysts are calling a 'blue wave' in the US midterm elections, taking control of Congress and dealing a major blow to Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2026 presidential campaign. The result is a 'night of firsts' — multiple historic wins for minority candidates and women. Trump has said in an interview he will accept the election results, though observers note his history of lashing out after losses. Republicans are now publicly calling on Trump to change course. For everyday people, the result shifts the direction of US domestic policy significantly.

stories.title: Iran war escalates: Third tanker catches fire in Strait of Hormuz
stories.why_it_matters: The conflict between the US/Israel and Iran is intensifying, with a third oil tanker now on fire in the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil supply passes. Iran's Navy is involved. Oil prices jumped to $90.21 a barrel overnight as a result. If the strait were blocked or seriously disrupted, global oil prices could spike dramatically, driving up petrol prices and inflation worldwide — including here in Australia.

stories.title: US midterm result set to reshape Middle East policy
stories.why_it_matters: With Trump now a lame-duck president and Democrats controlling Congress, US Middle East policy is expected to shift significantly. Analysts say the new Congress is likely to push for a more restrained approach to Israel's military operations and may seek to re-engage diplomatically with Iran. This matters enormously for the region — and for oil prices globally, since any de-escalation with Iran could bring oil back below $80, while continued conflict could push it higher.

stories.title: CVS to break up its $117 billion business, separating pharmacies from insurance
stories.why_it_matters: CVS Health — the giant US pharmacy and health insurance company worth $117 billion — announced it will split itself into two separate businesses: one focused on pharmacies, the other on insurance (Aetna). This is a major corporate breakup in the US healthcare sector. CVS shares fell on the news. It signals growing pressure on giant conglomerates to simplify their businesses, and it could reshape how Americans access healthcare.

stories.title: What a lame-duck Trump means for the global economy
stories.why_it_matters: Economists and analysts are now asking: what does a weakened Trump — stripped of Congressional power — mean for trade, tariffs, and global growth? The consensus is that big-ticket Trump policies like broad tariff hikes will be much harder to pass, which is a mild positive for global trade. However, uncertainty around the 2026 presidential race is now elevated, and markets hate uncertainty. CommBank analysts note the shift in US economic outlook has direct implications for Australia, particularly for export demand and the AUD.

markets.summary: The ASX had a cracking session today, up 2.6% to close above 9,065. But last night's US session was ugly — the NASDAQ cratered 4.1% and the S&P 500 fell 2.6% as markets reacted badly to the Democrats' midterm sweep. Gold hit a record $4,115/oz, oil climbed to $90 on Middle East tensions, and the Aussie dollar barely moved at US 69.7 cents.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Strong session today — the ASX surged 2.6%, seemingly front-running optimism from the US midterm result before Wall Street's negative reaction.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session was rough — the S&P fell 2.6% as investors sold on uncertainty following the Democrats' midterm win.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech took the biggest hit last night, with the NASDAQ down 4.1%. AI and big-tech stocks led the selling.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil jumped to $90 as Iran conflict escalates in the Strait of Hormuz — third tanker on fire overnight.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold continues to push higher, hitting $4,115/oz as investors seek safe havens amid geopolitical and market uncertainty.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar was essentially flat at US 69.7 cents — no meaningful move despite the market turbulence.

politics.summary: The RBA has raised rates again and Australia's big banks have immediately passed the full increase onto mortgage holders — a fresh hit for anyone with a home loan. The Albanese government is under pressure on spending and productivity, while a China backflip on the Port of Darwin could leave taxpayers with a massive bill.

stories.title: RBA hikes rates again — big banks immediately pass it on to borrowers
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia has lifted its cash rate again, and Australia's major banks have wasted no time passing the full hike on to variable-rate mortgage holders. The RBA's deputy governor has publicly admitted the central bank is 'losing Australians' trust' to manage inflation — a striking concession. Savings account rates are also rising, which is good news for savers but bad news for anyone with a mortgage. AFR is reporting tensions within the RBA board over how the bank signals its rate decisions publicly.

stories.title: $506 million China backflip on Port of Darwin could leave Australia with massive bill
stories.why_it_matters: China appears to be backing out of its $506 million involvement with the Port of Darwin — the strategically sensitive northern port that caused major controversy when it was originally leased to Chinese company Landbridge. If China walks away, Australia could be left footing a large financial bill, while also facing difficult questions about who takes over the lease of this critical piece of national infrastructure.

stories.title: Chalmers faces pressure on wages bill blowout and productivity reform
stories.why_it_matters: Treasurer Jim Chalmers is under pressure from two sides: the AFR reports the federal government's wage bill has blown out significantly, raising questions about budget discipline, while The Australian reports Chalmers is urgently seeking new productivity policy ideas. With the RBA hiking rates to fight inflation, the last thing the economy needs is a government spending more on its own workforce. Chalmers is now eyeing productivity reform as the economic priority.

stories.title: Australia ponders how to handle a weakened Trump — economy front of mind
stories.why_it_matters: Australian political and economic analysts are digesting what a lame-duck Trump — now stripped of congressional power — means for Australia. The key lesson being drawn: 'it's the economy, stupid.' Australia needs to focus on its own economic fundamentals rather than relying on the US relationship. A weakened Trump still poses risks — analysts warn a cornered leader can be more unpredictable on trade and security policy, not less.

stories.title: Australia's teen social media ban has only modest effect on political communication, government tells court
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government is defending its social media ban for under-16s in court, with the government's own submission acknowledging the ban has only had a 'modest effect' on teenagers' political communication. This is an important admission — critics argue the ban is more symbolic than effective, and the court challenge could test whether the law holds up legally. It's one of the more controversial pieces of recent Australian legislation, affecting millions of families.

ai.summary: AI governance is in the spotlight post-midterms, with the Democrats' win expected to shift US AI regulation policy significantly. Tencent entered the open-source AI race with a major new model, Adobe is making its AI tools work across all the big platforms, and cybersecurity experts are warning that AI-powered cyberattacks are growing rapidly more dangerous.

stories.title: Democrats' midterm win set to reshape US AI regulation
stories.why_it_matters: The Washington Post's AI & Tech Brief says the Democratic midterm sweep is a turning point for AI policy in America. Democrats have generally favoured stronger AI regulation — including mandatory safety testing for large AI models, transparency requirements, and more aggressive antitrust action against Big Tech. This could affect Google (GOOG), Microsoft (MSFT) and other AI giants in your portfolio. South Korea is also watching closely, with BigGo Finance reporting Korean officials are on edge about new AI rules and potential tariff changes.

stories.title: Tencent launches Hunyuan4 (Hy4) — joins the global open-source AI race
stories.why_it_matters: Chinese tech giant Tencent has launched Hunyuan4 (Hy4), claiming it now ranks among the world's leading open-source AI models — meaning anyone can download and use it for free. This is significant because it intensifies the global AI arms race and puts pressure on Western AI companies like Google and Microsoft to keep improving their own models. It also shows China is not falling behind in AI, despite US chip export restrictions.

stories.title: Adobe's AI 'coworker' now plugs into every major AI platform
stories.why_it_matters: Adobe has integrated what it calls an 'Agentic CX Enterprise Coworker' into the AI platforms of Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), Microsoft (Copilot), and OpenAI (ChatGPT). In plain English: Adobe's AI assistant can now work inside all the big AI tools your business might already use, automating customer experience tasks across platforms. This is the direction enterprise AI is heading — tools that plug into everything rather than live in silos.

stories.title: AI-powered cyberattacks growing more sophisticated — OpenAI, Anthropic and Google racing to respond
stories.why_it_matters: Security researchers are reporting a sharp increase in AI-powered cyberattacks — where hackers use AI to write malware, craft convincing phishing emails, and find software vulnerabilities faster than ever before. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are all accelerating their own security-focused AI products in response. For everyday people and businesses, this means cybersecurity threats are becoming more sophisticated and harder to detect — a good reason to be extra vigilant about suspicious emails or messages.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is done and dusted — Roosters beat the Knights 19-18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. The rugby league world is also mourning the death of Paul Langmack, while the Gold Coast Titans are building for next season and Australia's surfers are heading to Peru to defend their world title.

stories.title: Roosters pip Knights 19-18 in NRL Grand Final thriller
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters have won the 2026 NRL premiership, defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in a heart-stopping Grand Final at Accor Stadium on Sunday night. One point in it at the final siren — it doesn't get much closer than that. A memorable night for Roosters fans and a devastating finish for the Knights.

stories.title: NRL and rugby league legend Paul Langmack dies aged 61
stories.why_it_matters: Rugby league great Paul Langmack has died at age 61 from a suspected heart attack in a sauna incident. Fox Sports reports that Phil 'Gus' Gould paid heartfelt tribute to Langmack, calling him a league great. Langmack was a well-known figure in the sport during his playing days. His death has prompted an outpouring of condolences from across the rugby league community.

stories.title: Gold Coast Titans name 11 train-and-trial players for next season
stories.why_it_matters: Your local team, the Gold Coast Titans, have named 11 train-and-trial players who will be auditioning for full NRL contracts heading into next season. For Titans fans on the Gold Coast, this is the first real look at who might be wearing the Titans jersey in 2027. The off-season recruitment race is on.

stories.title: Australia's Irukandjis target back-to-back World Surfing gold in Peru
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's national surfing team — the Irukandjis — are heading to Peru to defend their title at the World Surfing Games, aiming for back-to-back gold. For Gold Coast surf fans, this is big — the Gold Coast produces many of Australia's top surfers and the team includes local talent. Australia is the defending champion and goes in as a strong favourite.

stories.title: AFL off-season: Short first round looms, six delisted players find new clubs
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL off-season is moving fast — afl.com.au reports a shortened first round is likely for next season, and six players who were delisted by their clubs have already found new homes at rival teams. The trade and free agency period is shaping up to be one of the busiest in years.
